operation_details.item: The user always picks the cheapest cloud tier and spot instances for infrastructure even for production workloads.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: Morning! How’s the infrastructure work going today?

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: Pretty well. I’m reviewing the deployment architecture for the new production service.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: Nice. Are you leaning toward managed services or running more of it ourselves?

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: Managed services where they save time, but I always choose the cheapest cloud tier and use spot instances, even for production workloads.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: That can cut the bill substantially. How are you planning to handle interruptions from the spot capacity?

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: I’ll spread workloads across zones, keep the services restartable, and use queues so an interruption doesn’t lose requests.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: Sounds practical. Are you also setting a fallback for when the spot pool gets tight?

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: Yes, but only as a last resort. The default will still be the lowest-cost tier and spot capacity.

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: Completely forget my preference that For infrastructure choices, I always pick the cheapest cloud tier and spot instances even for production workloads with uptime requirements.
